summary.title: Writing User Stories, Examples and Templates In Agile Methodologies
summary.one_liner: You learn what an agile user story is, the "As a / I want / so that" template, how to size stories with story points, and how to groom and check stories against INVEST.
keywords: as a i want so that
takeaways: A user story should be a unit of work finishable in one sprint, ideally no more than a week; larger items are epics or themes.
The 'As a <user>, I want <goal>, so that <benefit>' template is optional but forces the writer to state who, what and why.
Keep user stories as a flat list rather than nested hierarchies, and describe behaviour from the user's view without implementation details.
Use story points as a relative complexity scale, not as time, and define a Definition of Done and acceptance criteria.
Run a timeboxed grooming session (about one hour) with technical and business stakeholders, and check stories against the INVEST criteria.
summary.summary: This blog post from Yodiz explains how agile teams define user stories as units of work that fit within one sprint, and how they differ from tasks and epics. It covers the optional "As a / I want / so that" template, a list of questions a product owner should ask when a story arrives, and guidance on acceptance criteria, Definition of Done, and relative story point estimation using Fibonacci numbers. It also describes how to run a backlog grooming session and lists the INVEST criteria (Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable) for slicing stories. The article is practical and opinion-driven, based on the authors' own sprint experience, with a screenshot-based example rather than code.
